nodes.obligation: Prove the three parts: for every g there is a least positive k with g^k in H and k divides every m with g^m in H; if H is normal then k divides [G:H]; and a counterexample with H non-normal where k does not divide the index.
reader_obligations: Keep in view that part (a) must be proved without quotient-group machinery, since H is not assumed normal until part (b).

nodes.obligation: Define T = {m in Z : g^m in H} and see it as the preimage of H under the homomorphism m ↦ g^m from Z to G, so that membership m in T is exactly g^m in H.
reader_obligations: Recognize T as a preimage of a subgroup under a homomorphism; no minimality argument has happened yet.

nodes.obligation: Use finite index to produce a positive n with g^n in H: among the n+1 cosets H, gH, ..., g^nH two coincide, so g^(b-a) is in H for some 0 ≤ a < b ≤ n. This is the only place the finite-index hypothesis enters part (a).
reader_obligations: See that without finite index no positive exponent need exist (g of infinite order, H trivial), so this step carries all the finiteness.

nodes.obligation: Conclude T is a nonzero subgroup of Z, hence cyclic: T = aZ with a ≠ 0, because T contains the positive integer from the pigeonhole step.
reader_obligations: Recall that a subgroup of Z is the set of multiples of its generator, here the integer a with |a| the least positive element.

nodes.obligation: Read off the membership criterion with k = |a|: for every integer m, positive or negative, g^m in H if and only if k divides m.
reader_obligations: Check both directions: k | m puts g^m = (g^k)^(m/k) in H, and g^m in H forces m into aZ = T.

nodes.obligation: Conclude part (a): k = |a| is positive, g^k is in H, it is least among positive exponents that land in H, and it divides every integer m with g^m in H.
reader_obligations: See that minimality is a corollary of divisibility: a smaller positive exponent in H would be a positive multiple of k below k.

anchors.ref: Therefore $k$ is the smallest positive integer with $g^k\in H$

nodes.obligation: Under normality, form the quotient group G/H of order [G:H] and get g^[G:H] in H: the coset gH has order k by part (a), and Lagrange says the order of an element divides the order of the group.
reader_obligations: See that normality is used exactly here: it is what makes the coset space a group, so that Lagrange applies to the coset gH.

nodes.obligation: Apply the membership criterion of part (a) to the integer m = [G:H]: since g^[G:H] is in H, k divides [G:H].
reader_obligations: Watch the shape of the move: part (b) adds no new group theory, it feeds one specific integer into the criterion from part (a).

nodes.obligation: Set up the counterexample: G = S_3, H the subgroup generated by the transposition (0 1); H has order 2 and index 3, and it is not normal, witnessed by conjugating the generator to another transposition outside H.
reader_obligations: Verify the non-normality witness concretely: the conjugate of the generating transposition by another transposition is a third transposition, not in H.

nodes.obligation: Take g to be the transposition (0 2): g is not in H, g^2 = e is in H, so its least positive exponent is k = 2, while the index is 3 and 2 does not divide 3 — the conclusion of part (b) fails for non-normal H.
reader_obligations: Understand why this element and not a 3-cycle: an involution has k = 2 against an index-3 subgroup, and 2 does not divide 3.
